quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on the two statements, the journal, the ledger and the meaning of debit and credit.

questions.q: Which statement answers the question ‘how did we do this month?’
questions.explain: The profit and loss account shows the net profit or loss from the transactions of a period. The balance sheet shows the position on a fixed date, not performance over time.

questions.q: The balance sheet shows…
options: The net profit for the month
The financial position of the business on a fixed date
The debit and credit totals of each account
questions.explain: A balance sheet is a snapshot ‘as at’ a date: what the business owns and owes. Net profit belongs to the P&L; transactions in date order are in the journal.

questions.q: A balance sheet covers a period of time, such as a month.
questions.explain: The balance sheet is drawn ‘as at month end’ — a single date. It is the profit and loss account that covers a period.

questions.q: The journal records entries…
questions.explain: The journal is the day-book: entries in date order. The ledger then collects them account by account.

questions.q: The ledger is the book in which entries are…
options: Collected account by account in T-accounts
questions.explain: The ledger holds the T-accounts, one per account (Cash, Equipment, Sales and so on). Date-order recording is the journal’s job.

questions.q: The purpose of a trial balance in debit/credit form is to check that…
questions.explain: Since every entry has a debit and an equal credit, the sum of all debit balances must equal the sum of all credit balances — 21,550 each in Ahmed’s case.

questions.q: An increase in an asset such as cash is recorded as a…
questions.explain: Property (assets) increases on the debit side and decreases on the credit side. The opposite applies to liabilities and capital.

questions.q: An increase in the owner’s capital is recorded as a debit.
questions.explain: Capital is a right to property, and rights to property increase on the credit side. Ahmed’s Rs 19,000 deposit was credited to Ahmed, Capital.

questions.q: In the Cash T-account, ‘31 Balance c/d 2,100’ followed by ‘Jan 1 Balance b/d 2,100’ means…
options: The closing balance is carried down to close the month and brought down as the opening balance of the next
questions.explain: The balance carried down (c/d) makes the two sides total 21,000; the same figure is brought down (b/d) as the opening debit balance on 1 January.

questions.q: Which of these appears in the profit and loss account rather than the balance sheet?
questions.explain: Depreciation expense (200) is a cost of the month and goes to the P&L. Accumulated depreciation and equipment are balance-sheet items, and drawings are deducted from capital on the balance sheet.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How profit, capital and the balance sheet totals are linked, and which side each entry goes on.

questions.q: Net profit for the month is calculated as…
questions.explain: Net profit = sales − operating expenses (2,000 − 1,300 = 700). Assets minus liabilities gives capital, not profit.

questions.q: Closing capital on the balance sheet is built up as…
questions.explain: Capital 19,000 add profit 700 less withdrawals 500 = 19,200. Using sales instead of profit ignores the expenses.

questions.q: A business has sales of Rs 4,800 and total operating expenses of Rs 3,250. What is its net profit?
The correct journal entry for paying Rs 300 to trade creditors is…
questions.explain: The liability decreases (debit Trade Creditors) and the asset cash decreases (credit Cash). Reversing the sides would record the supplier being owed more.

questions.q: Why is an expense such as wages recorded as a debit?
options: Because expenses decrease capital, and a decrease in a right to property is a debit
Because all cash transactions are debits
questions.explain: Expenses reduce capital; capital is a right to property, and such rights decrease on the debit side. The matching credit is to Cash, which falls.

questions.q: Every journal entry has a debit and an equal credit.
questions.explain: This is the double-entry rule stated in the lecture; it is why the trial balance totals must agree.

questions.q: If expenses rise while sales stay the same, what happens to net profit and closing capital?
questions.explain: Higher expenses cut profit, and profit is added to capital on the balance sheet, so closing capital falls by the same amount.

questions.q: Which account normally carries a credit balance?
questions.explain: Accumulated depreciation (200) sits on the credit side of the trial balance as a deduction from the equipment asset. Cash, equipment and drawings are debit balances.

questions.q: Opening capital is Rs 45,000, net profit for the year Rs 6,200 and withdrawals Rs 3,500. What is closing capital?
Sales of Rs 2,000 are credited to the Sales account because…
options: Sales are a liability to customers
Income increases capital, and increases in rights to property are credits
questions.explain: Income increases the owner’s right to property, so it is credited; the debit goes to Cash, which increases.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Balance the T-accounts and build a profit and loss account and balance sheet from the figures.

questions.q: The Cash account has debits of Rs 19,000 (capital) and Rs 2,000 (sales), and credits of Rs 17,400, Rs 300, Rs 700 and Rs 500. What is the closing cash balance?
questions.explain: Debits 21,000 − credits 18,900 = Rs 2,100, the balance c/d on the credit side.

questions.q: Equipment cost Rs 17,400 and accumulated depreciation is Rs 200. At what figure does equipment appear on the balance sheet?
questions.explain: Equipment less accumulated depreciation = 17,400 − 200 = Rs 17,200.

questions.q: The debit balances are Cash Rs 2,100, Equipment Rs 17,400, Supplies Rs 250, expenses Rs 1,300 and Drawings Rs 500. What is the total of the debit side of the trial balance?
A workshop records sales Rs 12,000, wages Rs 4,200, rent Rs 1,000, supplies expense Rs 1,350, depreciation Rs 600, utilities Rs 310 and misc Rs 140. What is the net profit?
The same workshop has cash Rs 8,400, supplies Rs 900, equipment Rs 40,000 and accumulated depreciation Rs 1,200. What are its total assets?
Total liabilities and capital are Rs 48,100 and trade creditors are Rs 2,300. What is the closing capital?
Capital at the start of the month was Rs 42,500, profit was Rs 4,400 and closing capital is Rs 45,800. How much did the owner withdraw?
questions.explain: Withdrawals = opening + profit − closing = 42,500 + 4,400 − 45,800 = Rs 1,100.

questions.q: In a debit/credit trial balance, which of these balances is listed on the credit side?
questions.explain: Creditors are a liability with a credit balance. Supplies and drawings are debits, and expenses are debit balances too.

questions.q: The Trade Creditors account is credited with Rs 650 for supplies bought and debited with Rs 300 paid. What is the balance on the account?
questions.explain: Credit 650 − debit 300 = Rs 350 credit balance, shown as a liability.

questions.q: Which journal entry correctly records Rs 200 of depreciation on equipment?
options: Debit Depreciation Expense 200, credit Accumulated Depreciation 200
Debit Accumulated Depreciation 200, credit Depreciation Expense 200
questions.explain: The expense is debited and the contra-asset Accumulated Depreciation is credited. No cash is paid, so Cash is not involved.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Which statement to reach for, how to post everyday mill transactions, and the errors a trial balance will and will not catch.

questions.q: A mill owner wants to know whether there is enough cash to pay next week’s wages and the yarn supplier. Which statement should he read?
questions.explain: Cash on hand and creditors falling due are balance-sheet items. The P&L tells him whether the month was profitable, not what he holds tonight.

questions.q: A bank considering a loan asks whether the mill made money last year. Which statement answers this?
questions.explain: Profit over a period is the P&L’s question. The balance sheet shows position at a date, and the trial balance is an internal check.

questions.q: A clerk posts a Rs 17,400 equipment purchase as a debit to Equipment and also a debit to Cash. What will happen?
options: The trial balance debits will exceed credits by Rs 34,800
questions.explain: Cash should have been credited. Two debits and no credit leave the debit column 17,400 too high and the credit column 17,400 too low — a gap of 34,800.

questions.q: A weaving mill receives yarn worth Rs 500,000 from a spinner on credit. The journal entry is…
options: Debit Trade Creditors, credit Yarn Stock
Debit Yarn Stock, credit Trade Creditors
questions.explain: An asset (yarn) increases — debit; a liability (creditors) increases — credit. No cash moves and the owner’s capital is not affected.

questions.q: If the profit and loss account shows a net loss, the loss is added to capital on the balance sheet.
questions.explain: A profit is added to capital; a loss is deducted. Otherwise the balance sheet would not balance.

questions.q: The owner withdraws Rs 10,000 from the business bank account. The correct entry is…
questions.explain: Drawings reduce the owner’s right to property (debit) and cash falls (credit). Posting it as wages would wrongly reduce profit.

questions.q: A mill’s looms cost Rs 9,000,000 and accumulated depreciation is Rs 3,000,000. At what net figure do the looms appear on the balance sheet?
questions.explain: Net book value = 9,000,000 − 3,000,000 = Rs 6,000,000, shown as cost less accumulated depreciation.

questions.q: Which error will NOT be revealed by a trial balance that agrees?
options: Debiting Equipment but forgetting the credit to Cash
Posting rent paid to the Wages account instead of Rent
Adding up the debit column wrongly
Entering a debit of 700 and a credit of 70
questions.explain: Posting to the wrong account on the correct side keeps debits equal to credits, so the trial balance still agrees. The other three create unequal totals.

questions.q: Paying the month’s rent in cash reduces both an asset and the owner’s capital.
questions.explain: Cash (asset) falls and rent expense reduces capital. The entry is debit Rent Expense, credit Cash.

questions.q: Equipment was bought for Rs 17,400 and depreciated by Rs 200. How should it be presented after one month?
options: As an expense of Rs 17,400 in the P&L
On the balance sheet at Rs 17,400 less accumulated depreciation Rs 200
On the balance sheet at Rs 17,400 with no deduction
questions.explain: The balance sheet shows cost less accumulated depreciation (17,200). Only the Rs 200 depreciation goes to the P&L, not the whole cost.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step questions linking the journal, ledger, trial balance and the two statements.

questions.q: Which group of accounts all carry debit balances in Ahmed’s trial balance?
options: Equipment, Accumulated Depreciation, Drawings, Rent Expense
Trade Creditors, Sales, Capital, Accumulated Depreciation
questions.explain: Assets, drawings and expenses are debit balances. Sales, capital, creditors and accumulated depreciation are credit balances — the fourth option is the full credit side.

questions.q: Ahmed’s sales were Rs 2,000 and expenses Rs 1,300 including Rs 200 depreciation. If depreciation had been Rs 400 instead, with opening capital Rs 19,000 and drawings Rs 500, what would closing capital be?
questions.explain: Expenses become 1,500, profit = 2,000 − 1,500 = 500, closing capital = 19,000 + 500 − 500 = Rs 19,000.

questions.q: Ahmed’s debit/credit trial balance totals Rs 21,550 but his balance sheet totals Rs 19,550. Why are they different?
options: The trial balance contains an error of Rs 2,000
The trial balance lists sales, expenses, drawings and accumulated depreciation separately, while the balance sheet nets them into capital and equipment
The balance sheet omits the creditors
Drawings were not recorded on the balance sheet
questions.explain: The balance sheet shows net profit (sales − expenses) and drawings inside capital, and equipment net of depreciation. Those nettings remove 2,000 from each side; nothing is missing.

questions.q: A debit entry always means an increase.
questions.explain: A debit increases an asset but decreases a liability or capital. Debiting Trade Creditors by 300 reduced what Ahmed owed.

questions.q: Which of these journal entries is wrong?
options: Debit Cash 2,000, credit Sales 2,000 for cash sales
Debit Supplies 650, credit Trade Creditors 650 for supplies bought on credit
Debit Cash 500, credit Drawings 500 for the owner’s withdrawal
Debit Supplies Expense 400, credit Supplies 400 for supplies used
questions.explain: A withdrawal reduces cash, so Cash must be credited and Drawings debited. The entry shown would record cash coming in.

questions.q: Closing capital this month is Rs 19,200. Next month sales are Rs 3,000, expenses Rs 1,900 and drawings Rs 800. What is capital at the end of next month?
Which of these errors still leaves the trial balance in agreement?
options: Omitting the Rs 300 payment to creditors entirely
Recording the Rs 300 payment as a debit to Cash and a debit to Creditors
Entering the Rs 300 as 30 on the credit side only
questions.explain: An omitted transaction leaves both sides equally short, so the totals still agree. The other errors put different amounts on the two sides.

questions.q: On which side of the Cash T-account does ‘Jan 1 Balance b/d 2,100’ appear, and why?
options: Credit, because it closes the account
Debit, because cash is an asset and an asset balance is a debit
Credit, because it is owed to the owner
Debit, because all opening entries are debits
questions.explain: Cash is property; its balance is a debit. The balance c/d of 2,100 was written on the credit side only to make the two sides total 21,000.

questions.q: The net profit from the profit and loss account is the figure that links it to the balance sheet.
questions.explain: The 700 net profit is carried into the balance sheet as ‘add profit for the month’, which is why both sides then total 19,550.

questions.q: Supplies of Rs 650 were bought and the stock take shows only Rs 150 left instead of Rs 250. With sales Rs 2,000 and other expenses Rs 900, what are the supplies expense and the net profit?
questions.explain: Supplies used = 650 − 150 = 500; expenses = 900 + 500 = 1,400; profit = 2,000 − 1,400 = Rs 600. The supplies left (150) is the asset, not the expense.
